newsitem.title: INDIA: India, Bangladesh sign landmark water treaty.
newsitem.headline: India, Bangladesh sign landmark water treaty.

text.p: India and Bangladesh signed a new treaty to share water from the Ganges River on Thursday, which the leaders hailed as a stepping stone to improved relations between the South Asian neighbours.
Indian Prime Minister H.D. Deve Gowda and Prime Minister Sheikh Hasina of Bangladesh signed the 30-year treaty hours before Hasina left for home, ending a three-day visit to India.

"It is a matter of profound satisfaction for me that we have succeeded in finding a solution to something which has been an irritant for over two decades," Deve Gowda said at a joint news conference addressed by the two leaders.
"This is a moment of high emotion for me," said Hasina. "It is an event of such high significance that it will influence the course of bilateral relations for many years to come."
The treaty was expected to give a boost to Hasina, who, like Deve Gowda, assumed power in June following general elections.
"The key merit of this formula is that it shares available waters on a basis which is fair and equitable," Deve Gowda said in parliament after signing the agreement.

Bangladesh and a large portion of northern India depend on water from the Ganges. The level of water can vary dramatically, flooding large areas during the monsoon season or falling to dangerously low levels during the January-June dry period.

In 1977, the two nations signed an agreement to allow Bangladesh a guaranteed minimum of 34,000 cubic feet per second (cusecs) between October and June every year. But the guarantee was dropped in a new six-year accord signed in 1982.
Dhaka and New Delhi shared a cosy relationship after Bangladesh, formerly East Pakistan, achieved independence from Pakistan in 1971. India's army had helped Bangladesh's independence fighters.

But a simmering water dispute grew into a major source of friction after India built the Farakka Barrage in 1974, a dam that curbed the flow of the Ganges, which irrigates much of northern India before flowing into Bangladesh.
Bangladesh had charged that the dam, near the two countries' border, held back too much water during the annual dry season and released too much during monsoon rains, causing flooding.
Under the new treaty, if the water flow at Farakka is below 70,000 cusecs, as it usually is between March and May every year, the nations will split the water equally.
If the flow is between 70,000 and 75,000 cusecs, then Bangladesh will receive 35,000 with the rest going to India. Above 75,000 cusecs, India will be guaranteed 40,000 cusecs and Bangladesh the rest.
The accord is to be reviewed every five years.

India's opposition leader, Atal Behari Vajpayee of the Bharatiya Janata Party (BJP), said he welcomed improved relations with Bangladesh but cautioned, "We can talk about the accord only after reading (the details of) the statement."

Deve Gowda and Hasina thanked Jyoti Basu, the communist chief minister of India's West Bengal state, who played a key role in negotiating the treaty. West Bengal, which borders Bangladesh, is heavily dependent on the Ganges.
Deve Gowda also promised 1.0 billion rupees ($28.5 million) as aid to help bilateral trade which he said would be boosted by recent import tariff cuts offered by India to Bangladesh.

Hasina thanked India for the help it gave to her father, independence leader Sheikh Mujibur Rahman, but said in response to a question that there was no need to renew a 25-year-old friendship treaty that he signed with India in 1972.
She said the subsequent formation of the South Asian Association of Regional Cooperation (SAARC) covered the same areas as the earlier treaty.
